newsitem.title: USA: UAW strike deadline nears at GM parts plants.
newsitem.headline: UAW strike deadline nears at GM parts plants.

text.p: General Motors Corp. and the United Auto Workers union appeared headed for another labor clash on Friday night as they worked toward a midnight (0400 GMT) strike deadline at two Michigan auto parts plants.
An official at UAW Local 735 said union bargainers are not optimistic a new contract can be reached with GM for the 5,300 workers at transmission and components plants in Ypsilanti and Romulus, Mich.
"The sentiment is we're going to walk," said Charlie Copland, first vice president for the local. "As far as right now goes, they said, 'Get your walking shoes on.'"

A strike at the plant would have a faster and more widespread effect than a walkout at another transmission and parts plant in Warren, Mich., last month that idled six plants and 17,000 workers, Copland said. Several other GM plants depend on parts from Ypsilanti and Romulus for their production lines.

Negotiations aimed at averting a strike have stretched from early morning until past midnight every day this week. If no agreement is reached by the 11:59 p.m. deadline on Friday, union leaders will have the option of calling a strike or extending the deadline.
GM spokesman Charles Licari said the company remains hopeful it can reach a new contract without a work stoppage.

Negotiators for GM and UAW Local 22 avoided a strike last week by reaching a new pact for 3,600 workers at GM's Cadillac assembly plant in Detroit three hours after a midnight deadline expired on Aug. 8.

Most of Local 735's members work at GM's sprawling complex in Ypsilanti, known as the Willow Run facility. The plant makes transmissions for rear-wheel drive and front-wheel drive GM vehicles, including the Cadillac plant in Detroit.
It also turns out components for several other GM parts and assembly plants, including Warren, and a Toledo, Ohio, plant, which produces transmissions for most of GM's light trucks.

GM's Adam Opel unit in Germany and Rolls-Royce Plc also receive components from the plant, Copland said. About 300 of the local's members work at a satellite plant called Romulus Transmission Operation.
The disagreements between Local 735 and GM are the same issues that have separated the UAW and company all year, leading to six strikes and numerous other down-to-the-wire contract negotiations.
Local union officials are demanding that GM add more jobs to cut back on overtime costs, address health and safety concerns, and limit how much work it sends to outside contractors.
"It's ridiculous. They've got guys working 18 hours a day, seven days a week," said Copland, who declined to specify how many jobs the union wants added.

GM, which is trying to produce vehicles more efficiently, is determined not to add workers and shrink its workforce through attrition. Although a new national agreement was signed last November, eight of GM's 105 UAW locals still do not have new contracts.

Employment at the Willow Run complex, one of the largest GM has, has dropped more than half from the approximately 12,000 workers it had 20 years ago. The transmission operation is part of the mile-long facility that was originally constructed to build B-24 bombers during World War II.
